drills.q: Explain structural vs nominal typing and why an object literal can satisfy an interface it never declared implementing.
drills.a: TypeScript checks whether a value's shape is compatible with a target type -- same or superset of required properties with compatible types -- regardless of any declared name or inheritance relationship. An object literal satisfies an interface purely by having the right shape, with no `implements` requirement.

drills.q: Why does distance({x:3,y:4,z:5}) error as an excess property but distance(someVarWithExtraProps) does not?
drills.a: Excess property checks fire specifically on object literals passed directly, to catch likely typos in property names. They don't apply to variables holding an object with genuinely extra properties -- a deliberately narrower check than full structural strictness would imply.

drills.q: What does 'types are erased' mean, and what's the practical consequence for runtime safety?
drills.a: Every type annotation, interface, and generic parameter is deleted during compilation to JS -- zero runtime trace. TypeScript can never enforce anything at runtime; a value crossing an unchecked boundary (an as assertion, untyped import, stale third-party .d.ts) can be structurally wrong at runtime while the type checker reports everything fine.

drills.q: Distinguish unknown from any mechanically, and state where TypeScript itself defaults to unknown as of 4.4+.
drills.a: Both accept any assigned value. any disables type checking entirely for anything it touches -- propagates silently downstream. unknown requires explicit narrowing (typeof/instanceof/custom guard) before any operation. TS 4.4+ types caught errors in catch clauses as unknown by default (useUnknownInCatchVariables), since a thrown value's type is never knowable ahead of time.

drills.q: Write a discriminated union for a fetch state (idle/loading/success/error) and explain why it beats one flat interface with optional fields.
drills.a: type FetchState<T> = {status:'idle'} | {status:'loading'} | {status:'success',data:T} | {status:'error',error:string}. A flat interface with optional data/error/loading fields allows illegal combinations to compile (e.g. loading:true with stale data present) -- a real, common stale-UI bug. The discriminated union makes that structurally impossible since fields only exist in the branch's type where they're valid.

drills.q: How do you force the compiler to catch a missed case when a new discriminated union variant is added later?
drills.a: Add a const _exhaustive: never = value; statement in the default/fallback branch of the switch. If a new variant isn't handled, value in that branch is no longer assignable to never, producing a compile error instead of a silent runtime fallthrough.

drills.q: Why is an `as` type assertion dangerous, and when is it legitimately acceptable to use?
drills.a: It performs zero runtime verification -- if the value isn't actually shaped as claimed, it compiles fine and the mismatch surfaces later, often far from the assertion site. Legitimate use: narrowing a type the compiler can't infer but you can prove safe from context it doesn't see (e.g. a querySelector result's more specific element type when you control the DOM), not silencing an error whose underlying concern is real.

drills.q: Explain function parameter bivariance in TypeScript: what's unsafe by default, what fixes it, and what carve-out remains even under strict mode.
drills.a: Without strictFunctionTypes, (x:Dog)=>void is assignable to (x:Animal)=>void and vice versa, even though only contravariance (accepting a wider parameter) is actually safe. strictFunctionTypes (part of strict mode) fixes this for standalone function types. Method syntax (interface Foo { method(x:Dog):void }) remains bivariant even under strict mode -- a deliberate, documented compatibility carve-out.

drills.q: What is declaration merging, give a legitimate production use, and explain its risk.
drills.a: Multiple interface declarations with the same name across files automatically merge into one combined interface. Legitimate use: augmenting a global or third-party type (e.g. adding a property Express's Request gets from auth middleware) without forking the library's types. Risk: it declares a runtime shape exists with zero verification anything actually sets it -- if the middleware doesn't run on some route, the type still claims the field exists, and access crashes at runtime with no compile-time warning.

drills.q: Derive Pick<T,K> and Partial<T> as mapped types from first principles, without reciting their documented behavior.
drills.a: Pick<T,K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] } -- iterates the keys in K, pulling each corresponding property type from T. Partial<T> = { [P in keyof T]?: T[P] } -- same iteration over all of T's keys with the ? modifier applied.

drills.q: A third-party library's .d.ts claims a field is always present, but production shows it's sometimes undefined. How did this happen, and what's the fix without waiting on upstream?
drills.a: The .d.ts (bundled or from @types/*) was written by hand or generated against a different version/behavior than what's shipping, and TypeScript has no mechanism to verify a .d.ts file's accuracy against actual runtime behavior -- it's trusted completely. Fix: locally patch via declare module augmentation to reflect actual observed behavior (mark the field optional), and defensively handle the value (optional chaining, runtime checks) regardless of the stale type's claim.

drills.q: What is TypeScript 6.0's significance as 'the last JS-based release,' and what does TypeScript 7.0 change (and not change)?
drills.a: 6.0 (March 2026) flipped defaults toward stricter behavior (broader strict defaults, ESM default module, es2025 target) and was explicitly a bridge release. TypeScript 7.0 is a from-scratch rewrite of the compiler in Go, reported ~10x faster, reaching RC June 18 2026 -- it's a reimplementation targeting build/editor speed, not a new language; the type system's semantics stay the same.
